Men and women have different tastes in art because of biological diversity that was forged in the Stone Age, according to a leading academic. And the fact early men and women took on the different roles of hunters and gatherers may explain why just one painting at the National Gallery is by a woman.

Prof Gloria Moss, an Australian professor and author, says that 15,000 years ago when the first cave paintings were made, men, being hunters, were out tracking animals and needed to be able to spot them against any background, which led to them developing good color vision.
But women, who stayed at home and gathered fruit and plants, could survive with less colour vision, and so developed colour blindness.

That difference continues today, says Moss. Men like paintings that are darker and have fewer colours, but women prefer paintings that are full of bright, bold colours and have people or flowers in it, she says. Moss wrote these things about in her 2016 book "The Artist's Eye."

In a BBC interview, Moss says, "What you see and what you do and how you make sense of what you see are all connected. And the difference is there for everybody."

Moss has a degree from Oxford University and a PhD from Cambridge University, so she knows a little something about brains.
